title: Zoning of retail trade in the diagnosis of retail service development in the Russian Federation and the Krasnoyarsk Krai
abstract: Subject. Processes of production and exchange of material goods, development of service business processes that have a significant impact on customer loyalty. Objectives. Development of a methodological framework for strategic zoning of retail trade, allowing the identification of territorial disparities in service quality. Methods. General scientific research methods were applied. Results. The possibility of integrating analytical models into retail zoning practice has been justified, which creates a basis for differentiated regulation of the development of the retail sector, taking into account both quantitative and qualitative characteristics. Conclusions. Identifying stable strategic zones creates a structural map of the market, where each segment reflects not only economic indicators but also a specific service logic, the depth of interaction with the consumer, and the nature of competitive advantages.

title: Venture capabilities, ecosystem conditioning and scaling pathways: evidence from technology startups in the Middle East
journal: Journal of Small Business and Enterprise Development
abstract: Purpose This research analyzes the impact of technology and technology-related startups operating within rapidly expanding, state-sponsored entrepreneurial ecosystems. While venture capabilities are often viewed as drivers of growth, little is known about how these capabilities are activated, validated and translated into scalable outcomes in contexts of strong state involvement and institutional transition. Using Saudi Arabia as the empirical setting, the study investigates how venture capabilities and ecosystem conditions interact to shape various scaling pathways. Design/methodology/approach The study draws on in-depth, semi-structured interviews with founders and senior executives from 26 Saudi technology and tech-enabled ventures. Using a Gioia-informed inductive approach, we developed a process-oriented analysis that links informant-voiced concepts to second-order themes and aggregate dimensions. Following an iterative review of the observed data structure, we propose a dynamic explanation of scaling pathways that are shaped by ecosystem conditioning mechanisms. Findings The findings show that scaling is a negotiated and path-dependent process rather than a direct outcome of ventures' capability. Thus, government support, accelerators, public procurement and ecosystem recognition can accelerate early growth, but they may also distort real signals by making supported milestones appear similar to sustainable market validation. The findings also reveal a capability-outcome decoupling phenomenon, where ventures strengthen internal financial, operational, product and talent capabilities but struggle to convert them into sustained scaling because of procurement bottlenecks, conservative investment behavior, market-readiness gaps and talent constraints. Originality/value The study contributes to scaling research by proposing that scaling is a process of capability conversion, conditioned by the ecosystem. Furthermore, it extends resource-based and entrepreneurial ecosystem perspectives by showing how state-led ecosystem architectures shape the timing, credibility and validation of venture capabilities in emerging and policy-driven contexts.

title: The relationship between childhood traumatic life experiences and social anxiety disorders
abstract: Background: Childhood traumatic experiences are known to have profound and lasting effects on mental health; however, there are limited data on the relationship between types of childhood trauma and social anxiety in non-clinical populations. Aim: This study aimed to explore the associations between types of childhood trauma and social anxiety symptoms in non-clinical young adults. Setting: The study was conducted at the Faculty of Health Sciences of a university in Istanbul, Turkey. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 486 university students. Sample size was determined via G*Power analysis to ensure statistical power. Participants completed the Liebowitz Social Anxiety Scale (LSAS) and the Childhood Trauma Questionnaire (CTQ) to assess childhood trauma types and social anxiety symptoms. Data were analysed using stepwise multiple regression. Results: The mean age of the participants was 21.8 ± 4.0 years, and 81% were female, with emotional abuse and neglect scoring highest in both genders. The sample’s LSAS total mean score was 63.87 ± 11.68. When the subscales were compared by gender, females had significantly higher mean fear and avoidance scores than males (p < 0.05). The results show that childhood abuse and neglect were significant predictors of social anxiety and explained 23% of the social anxiety variance. Conclusion: Childhood abuse and neglect are clearly associated with social anxiety symptoms. Interventions and treatments for individuals with social anxiety should incorporate a detailed assessment of childhood trauma history, with a particular focus on emotional abuse and neglect. Contribution: This study contributes to the literature by clarifying the associations between specific types of childhood trauma and social anxiety symptoms in a non-clinical young adult population.

title: Service quality and student cynicism in higher education: the mediating role of perceived ethical climate
abstract: Purpose This study examines the mediating role of perceived ethical climate (PEC) in the relationship between service quality and student cynicism (SC) in higher education. This study aims to examine whether PEC explains the relationship between perceived institutional quality and students’ cynical attitudes. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 424 senior undergraduate students at a public university in Türkiye. Validated scales measuring service quality, PEC and SC were used. Confirmatory factor analyses supported the measurement models. The hypothesized mediation model was tested using bootstrapped regression analysis. Findings Service quality was negatively associated with SC and positively associated with PEC, while PEC was negatively related to cynicism. Mediation analysis indicated that PEC partially mediates the relationship between service quality and student cynicism. The findings suggest that quality-oriented institutional practices may reduce SC by strengthening the PEC. Originality/value This study makes three key contributions. First, it integrates service quality, PEC and SC into a single theoretically grounded model, addressing an important gap in the higher education literature. Second, it empirically demonstrates the mediating role of PEC as a mechanism linking institutional quality perceptions to student attitudes. Third, it offers practical implications for higher education governance by showing how aligning quality management practices with ethical principles can reduce student cynicism.

title: Family hands: remedy or poison? The curvilinear moderating role of family job involvement in hospitality entrepreneurs' job demands
abstract: Purpose In small businesses where entrepreneurs frequently involve family members, this study examines whether such involvement serves as a resource or a hindrance. Anchored in family embeddedness theory, this study proposes the curvilinear moderating effect of family members' job involvement on the relationship between job demands and satisfaction for entrepreneurs, mediated by work-family conflict (WFC) and work-family facilitation (WFF). Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from small business owners and their family members in Taiwan's hospitality sector, specifically bed and breakfast establishments. Structural equation modeling tested the mediated-moderation framework, capturing both linear and curvilinear effects. Findings The findings highlight the mediating role of WFF in the linkage between job demands and satisfaction for entrepreneurs. Intriguingly, the results reveal that the positive association between job demands and WFC intensifies at moderate levels of family members' job involvement, demonstrating a curvilinear moderating effect. Practical implications This study identifies governance and conflict-management strategies that owners can implement to manage varying levels of family involvement and improve coordination and satisfaction for entrepreneurs in small family-owned hospitality businesses. Originality/value By advancing the theoretical boundaries of family embeddedness theory, this study provides novel insights for understanding the dynamics of family-centric small businesses.
